newsitem.title: USA: Minimum wage hike kicks in -- with a thud.
newsitem.headline: Minimum wage hike kicks in -- with a thud.

text.p: Millions of Americans earning the minimum wage got a 50-cent an hour raise Tuesday but despite the election year hoopla that led up to it, the increase drew little notice.
It was news to Gino, a cashier at a deli in downtown Denver.
"Should I check with my boss on this?" he asked.

Many wage earners at the bottom of the ladder already make more than the $4.75 an hour that became the national standard Tuesday, and some are already making more than the $5.15 an hour to which the minimum will rise in 13 months.

"The minimum wage ought to be at least $5.50 nationally because $4.75 ain't nothin'," said a man waiting for work at Lake Land Temps, a day labour agency in Cleveland. "It just keeps you half-way alive, keeps you from starvin'."
Frank Spoth, president of Lake Land, said the increase will be passed through to his customers.
"It may hurt initially, but when people need temporary help, they need temporary help. So why worry?" he said. "As strong as the economy is today, I don't see anything hurting."

Jay Mazur, president of the New York-based Union of Needle Trades, Industrial and Textile Employees, called the increase "a small but significant step toward restoring the real earnings of American workers."
But he added, "We are still some distance from making up the 31 percent decline in the purchasing power of the minimum wage over the past 18 years."
In the thriving tourist mecca of Key West, Fla., the de facto minimum wage is already about $5.50 an hour.

"I'm happy for the ones who will get a little extra because it's hard to make it in Key West," said Lisa Carey, 28, a lifetime Key West resident and a checkout clerk at Faustos Food Palace, who said she was already making more than the minimum.

Kim Miller, a spokeswoman at Burger King's corporate headquarters in Miami, said the average wage paid to workers at company-owned restaurants was $6 an hour nationwide even before the increase. Wages in excess of the minimum are common across the fast food industry.

"I'm looking for a job, but I couldn't work for that. I would try public assistance before I'd go for that," said Janice Perkins, 38, who was filling out paperwork in a job placement office in Kansas City, Mo.
The number of people affected by the increase is open to question.
President Clinton, in pushing the first increase in five years through Congress, said it would give 10 million workers a raise.
But economist Robert Samuelson, in a recent commentary, called the 10 million figure doubtful.

He said there were 3.7 million people earning $4.25, the old minimum figure, in 1995 and another 2.2 million earning less than $4.70 an hour. Most of those 5.9 million will get the increase, though some are exempt, Samuelson said.
In the meantime, he added, wages are rising generally about 3 percent a year.
In Boston, George Rigby, who makes his living carrying a sandwich board advertisement for a one-hour photo shop near Government Centre, said:

"I won't work for minimum wage. It doesn't make any sense for a single man to work for minimum wage, when the government would take half of it in taxes anyway. Why, I couldn't keep my apartment on minimum wage."

Bill Rockwood, manager of Kerry's Kwik Stop in Burlington, Vt., said, "Probably the segment of the population impacted the most is going to be the high school students and kids looking for a part-time job ... those who need training coming right in off the street."
The manager of Edwards Superstore in Wakefield, R.I., who asked that his name not be used, said about 20 of his 80 workers were making minimum wage and "They're all kids who work after school."
One who did take notice was Diana Oviedo, a minimum wage pharmacy cashier in Miami.
"With every paycheck it's much better," said Oviedo, an 18-year-old college student. "When you work for minimum wage you feel like you're a slave. The more it goes up, the better I like it."

Elsewhere in Miami Piotr Krol, a 19-year-old student from Poland who recently quit a minimum wage job at a Miami restaurant, said "Fifty cents is nothing ... I was working hard, doing a good job. They wouldn't pay me any more so I quit."

In Los Angeles, Ralph Richeson, manager of The Bread Winner, a busy delicatessen that employs 12 people, said only a few delivery boys are paid minimum wage. But he worries about what the increase will do to the costs of his supplies, which he said "may rise as much as 20 percent."
A survey of small business owners released Tuesday by the Commerce Clearing House in Chicago found that only about half thought the increase was very or somewhat important.
Preston Gibson, 37, a sales representative in Pittsburgh, said:

"I used to work for minimum wage and I didn't like it so I got a real job. Nothing's given to anyone ... if you don't like working for minimum wage, then do the things you need to do to get off of it."
